kav1: Pain at the front of your leg when you run? What causes shin splints, how long should you rest, and how do you tell them apart from a stress fracture? Returning to running and six exercises to do at home.
kav3: Have you just started running, or stepped up your training quickly, and now feel an ache along the front of your shins? Shin splints are caused by too much load on the leg, usually from repeated impact such as running and jumping. They are not serious and often get better within a few weeks; what matters most is returning gradually without repeating the same mistake.

kav12: At first it is a dull ache; over time it can become sharp enough to stop you exercising, and may even continue at rest.

kav14: Starting exercise after a period of inactivity, or suddenly increasing the load.
kav15: Running or jumping on hard or uneven surfaces.

kav19: Take a break: Stop the activity that caused the pain for at least 2–3 weeks.
kav20: Ice: In the first few days, you can apply ice wrapped in a towel to your shin for 10–20 minutes every few hours.
kav21: Painkillers: Paracetamol or ibuprofen may help; if you are unsure, you can ask your pharmacist.
kav22: Stay active: Swimming, cycling, cross-trainers and yoga put less strain on the shins.
kav24: When the pain has gone, do not go straight back to your previous level; build up time and frequency gradually.
kav25: Run on flat, soft surfaces where possible.
kav27: Warm up before exercise, and afterwards stretch your calves and the front of your legs in particular.
kav28: Choose trainers that support your feet well and have enough cushioning.
kav29: Six exercises to strengthen the legs
kav30: Do the stretching and strengthening movements within a pain-free range. If the pain in your shin increases, reduce the load; if you get sharp pain in a small spot, stop the exercise and see your doctor.
kav31: Place your hands on a wall and step one leg back. Keeping the back knee straight and the heel on the floor, move your hips towards the wall until you feel a stretch in your calf. It is recommended after exercise.
kav34: Sit with your feet flat on the floor. Keeping your heels down, lift your toes, then lower them and lift your heels instead. It works the muscles at the front of the shin and in the calf without pain.
kav35: Stand upright holding the worktop. Rise up onto your toes on both feet, hold for 2 seconds and lower slowly. If it does not cause pain, you can progress to one foot over time.
kav36: Stand upright in front of the worktop, holding on lightly with one hand if needed. Lift one foot off the floor and keep your balance. As it gets easier, try without holding on or with your eyes closed.
kav39: It is recommended to take a break of at least two to three weeks from the activity that caused the pain, then return gradually. Meanwhile, you can stay active with movements that put less strain on the shins, such as swimming, cycling, a cross-trainer or yoga.
kav40: How do I know whether it is a stress fracture?
kav41: Shin splints usually affect both legs over an area wider than 5 centimetres. If the pain is focused on a small spot, is mostly in one leg and there is swelling, it may be a stress fracture. An X-ray can look normal at first; in that case, you can see your doctor.
kav43: If you have flat feet or feet that roll inwards, a podiatrist may suggest insoles. However, in research, shin splints were more common in people who used insoles; this may not mean insoles cause the pain, but that people already at risk are the ones using them. You can make the decision together with a specialist.
kav44: Who is more likely to get them?
kav45: They affect 5 to 35 per cent of runners. Research has found them more often in women, people with a higher body mass index, people whose foot arch drops markedly, people who have had the same pain before and people who are new to running.
